one_liner: Archived research AVX2 base64 codec from the Muła–Lemire paper; roughly 7-11x faster than Chrome's scalar codec on Skylake.
what_it_does: A small C99 collection of base64 encoders and decoders: the paper's AVX2 codec (fast_avx2_base64_encode/decode), an AVX-512BW variant, a POWER9 AltiVec port and a stand-alone NEON decoder file. Each one wraps Nick Galbreath's modp_b64 codec as used in Chromium and keeps its API: (char *dest, const char *src, size_t len) returns the bytes written or MODP_B64_ERROR, and the caller sizes buffers with the chromium_base64_encode_len/decode_len macros. It supports only the standard alphabet with '=' padding, and the decoder rejects any byte outside that alphabet, whitespace included. The repo also bundles the Linux kernel, QuickTime, plain scalar and Klomp AVX2 codecs, plus the benchmark used in the paper.
how_it_is_fast: Encoding: a vpshufb puts each 3-byte group into a 32-bit lane. A vpmulhuw/vpmullw multiply-shift then extracts all four 6-bit fields at once, and ASCII translation uses a saturating-subtract/compare range index into a 16-entry vpshufb offset table instead of a 64-byte lookup table. Decoding uses aqrit's nibble-LUT scheme: two vpshufb lookups on the high and low nibbles produce bitmasks whose vptest catches any invalid byte, and a third vpshufb supplies the per-range offset. Then vpmaddubsw + vpmaddwd pack four 6-bit values into 24 bits, and vpshufb + vpermd compact 32 characters into 24 bytes. The paper counts about 11 vector instructions per 24 input bytes for encoding and 14 per 32 for decoding, which is about 0.25 cycles/byte on Skylake. Tails shorter than 28 bytes (encode) or 45 characters (decode) go to the Chromium scalar code.
when_to_use: Reproducing or extending Muła & Lemire (ACM TWEB 2018): this repo is the paper's artifact, with basic_benchmark.c, the test images and the rival codecs in one harness.
Reading a minimal reference of the AVX2 base64 kernels (about 200 lines in src/fastavxbase64.c) before porting the technique into your own code.

Only if you must vendor a tiny C kernel and cannot take simdutf: strict, padded, whitespace-free standard-alphabet data of about 200 bytes or more (data URIs, embedded images) on AVX2 x86-64 that you build for yourself.
when_not_to_use: Anything in production: the README says it is unmaintained research code and not for production, the repo is archived, and the author sends users to simdutf.
MIME/PEM or other input with line breaks or spaces, URL-safe alphabet, or missing padding: the Chromium fallback returns MODP_B64_ERROR and there are no options.
Short strings: the paper says that under about 100 bytes the AVX2 codec is no faster than scalar code.
The AVX-512BW encoder: issue #17 (2024) reports garbage output for a 64-byte input on Sapphire Rapids while still returning the expected length. It was closed without a fix.

Non-x86 targets: the POWER9 AltiVec port is only about 2-2.4x Chrome at 2 KB (decode 0.32 vs 0.65 ns/byte, encode 0.27 vs 0.66), the NEON file is decode-only and not built by the Makefile, and there is no aarch64 encoder.

integration.min_toolchain: C99 compiler with AVX2 intrinsics; the paper used GCC 5.3 -O3 -march=native; the Makefile's -Wpsabi flag is GCC-only (clang warns)
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX2 (AVX-512BW variant optional); ppc64le POWER9 AltiVec port; NEON decoder source only; no runtime CPU dispatch
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The functions are stateless and read only static const tables (per the source), so concurrent calls on separate buffers look safe.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same signature and return convention as Chromium's modp_b64 (chromium_base64_encode/decode), so it swaps in where that API is used; not a drop-in for coreutils/glibc base64, OpenSSL or any whitespace-tolerant decoder

gotchas: No CPU detection: fast_avx2_* crashes with SIGILL on CPUs without AVX2, and the Makefile builds everything with -march=native, so the binaries are not portable.

Each decode step stores 32 bytes but advances only 24, so the region past the current output position gets scratch bytes. By our reading this stays inside a buffer sized for the decoded output. On invalid input the function returns MODP_B64_ERROR after writing partial output.

The encoder's first load is a masked vpmaskmovd from str-4 (that lane is masked, so no fault per Intel docs). Turbo-Base64's source calls fastbase64 'unsafe, can reads/writes beyound i/o buffers'; we did not confirm that for the AVX2 path, and the unit tests cover only three fixed strings plus an invalid-character sweep.
Decoding requires a length that is a multiple of 4. The header says encode returns strlen+1, but the code returns strlen and writes a NUL terminator.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: For real use, pick simdutf (maintained descendant of this algorithm, runtime dispatch, whitespace and URL-safe support), aklomp/base64 (maintained C99 library that adopted these kernels) or Turbo-Base64 (29,086/29,748 MB/s vs fastbase64's 23,686/21,231 MB/s encode/decode in the same i7-9700K table). Pick fastbase64 only to reproduce the paper or to read the smallest reference version of the AVX2 kernels.
verified_claims_summary: The paper measured on an i7-6700 Skylake at 3.4 GHz with Turbo off, GCC 5.3 -O3 -march=native, taking the minimum rdtsc count over 500 runs. There the AVX2 codec needs about 0.25 cycles/byte on large random inputs, against 2.7 (encode) and 1.8 (decode) for Chrome 56's modp_b64, and it decodes six real files at 0.21-0.27 cycles/byte against Chrome's 1.8-2.1 and Klomp AVX2's 0.43-0.53. In Turbo-Base64's independent 1 MB table (i7-9700K, gcc 11.2) fb64avx2 reaches 23,686/21,231 MB/s encode/decode against Chrome's 2,541/4,289, but by then it trails aklomp's b64avx2 (26,153/22,515).
status_note: Archived, with the last commit on 2024-04-04; the README and issue #17 call it obsolete and point to simdutf. The LICENSE file is standard BSD-2-Clause text (GitHub shows NOASSERTION), so vendoring is allowed, but every fix is yours.
